title: Gustar and Its Family
bigQuestion: How does Spanish talk about likes and dislikes when the thing you like is the subject of the sentence?

story.title: A Menu for Twenty
story.kicker: Planning one dinner for a big family means learning who likes what, and how to say it.
paragraphs: Abuela's seventieth birthday was two weeks away, and Lucía had volunteered to plan the menu. Twenty relatives were coming to the house in Little Village. She sat down with her notebook and her cousin Tomás. "Primero, ¿qué le gusta a Abuela?" (First, what does Grandma like?), she asked.

Tomás thought. "A Abuela le gustan los tamales" (Grandma likes tamales). "Y le encanta el mole" (And she loves mole). Lucía wrote it down. Then she frowned. "Pero a tío Raúl no le gusta el picante" (But Uncle Raúl doesn't like spicy food). "Y a las gemelas les molesta la cebolla" (And the onion bothers the twins).

Lucía noticed something strange. In English, she was the one doing the liking. In Spanish, the food seemed to be doing something to the person. "Me gustan los tamales" felt more like tamales are pleasing to me. The word for the food changed the verb: gusta for one thing, gustan for many.

They called their other cousins. "¿Te gusta el pozole?" (Do you like pozole?). "¡Sí, me encanta!" (Yes, I love it!). "A mí no me gusta" (I don't like it), said another. Tomás laughed. "A mí tampoco" (Me neither). The list grew with every call.

By the end of the night, Lucía had a menu: tamales, rice, beans, a mild mole and a spicy salsa on the side. "Nos falta el postre" (We're missing dessert), Tomás pointed out. Lucía smiled and wrote one more word: pastel. Everyone likes cake.
story.think: Why do you think Spanish says the food is pleasing to you instead of saying you like the food?

lessons.title: The Thing Liked Is the Subject
lessons.mainIdea: In me gusta el mole, el mole is the subject; the sentence means mole is pleasing to me.
reading: Picture Lucía's grandmother tasting mole and smiling. In English, you would say She likes mole. The person is the subject, and mole is the object. Spanish flips it: "Le gusta el mole." The verb *gustar* means to be pleasing, and the mole is doing the pleasing.

Read it word by word. Le (to her) gusta (is pleasing) el mole (the mole). So the *subject* of the sentence is el mole, the thing liked. The person who likes it appears as a small word before the verb that means to me, to you, to her. That word is called an *indirect object pronoun*.

This is why "Yo gusto el mole" is wrong, even though it copies English word order. Yo gusto would mean I am pleasing. The right sentence is "Me gusta el mole" (Mole is pleasing to me, I like mole). Once you think of gustar as to be pleasing, the rest of the pattern makes sense.

words.d: to be pleasing — used to say like: Me gusta el arroz (I like rice; rice is pleasing to me)
the subject — grammar word for who or what does the verb; with gustar it is the thing liked
grammar word: a small word (me, te, le, nos, os, les) that tells to whom or for whom something happens

look.title: Word by word
look.text:
English: I like mole.
Spanish: Me gusta el mole.
me = to me
gusta = is pleasing
el mole = the mole (the subject)
Literal: Mole is pleasing to me.
look.prompt: Translate word by word: Te gusta el pozole. What is the subject?

check.q: In the sentence "Me gusta la música", what is the subject?
check.why: With gustar, the thing liked is the subject. La música is what is pleasing.

check.q: How do you say "I like rice"?
check.why: Gustar agrees with the thing liked (el arroz), and the person appears as me: Me gusta el arroz.

check.q: What is the literal meaning of "Me gusta el fútbol"?
check.why: Gustar means to be pleasing: soccer is pleasing to me.

lessons.title: Gusta or Gustan
lessons.mainIdea: Use gusta with one thing or an infinitive, and gustan with more than one thing.
reading: Lucía writes "Me gustan los tamales" and "Me gusta el arroz." Why the n? Because the verb agrees with its subject, the thing liked. One rice: gusta. Many tamales: gustan. The person liking it never changes the verb ending. So the ending depends on what is liked, not on who likes it.

Activities work like one thing. When you like doing something, use gusta plus an infinitive: "Me gusta cocinar" (I like to cook). Even two activities stay singular: "Me gusta cocinar y bailar" (I like to cook and dance). Only plural nouns, like las canciones (the songs), take gustan.

The common mistake is choosing gustan because the PERSON is plural. "Nos gustan el pastel" is wrong, because el pastel is one thing: "Nos gusta el pastel" (We like the cake). Always look to the right of the verb, find the thing liked, and count it. Count it before you choose the ending.

words.d: I like (one thing or an activity) — Me gusta el pastel. Me gusta nadar.
I like (more than one thing) — Me gustan los tamales.
the infinitive — the -ar, -er, -ir form of a verb; with gustar it counts as one thing

look.title: Count what is liked
look.text:
Me gusta el mole. → el mole = one → gusta
Me gustan las tortillas. → las tortillas = many → gustan
Me gusta bailar. → an activity = one → gusta
Nos gusta la salsa. → la salsa = one → gusta (even though nos is plural)
look.prompt: Write one sentence with gusta and one with gustan about foods at a family party.

check.q: Which form completes the sentence? Me ___ los frijoles.
check.why: Los frijoles is plural, so gustar takes the plural form gustan.

check.q: Which form completes the sentence? Nos ___ el pastel de chocolate.
check.why: The thing liked, el pastel, is singular, so the verb is gusta even though nos is plural.

check.q: Which sentence is correct?
check.why: Infinitives count as one thing, even two of them together, so the verb is gusta.

lessons.title: Saying No and Asking
lessons.mainIdea: Put no right before the pronoun to make a negative, and turn the sentence into a question with ¿ ? around it.
reading: Uncle Raúl does not like spicy food. In Spanish, no goes in front of the whole pronoun-plus-verb group: "No me gusta el picante" (I don't like spicy food). Never split them. "Me no gusta" is a common error, because English puts not after the subject.

To ask, keep the same order and add question marks at both ends. "¿Te gusta el pozole?" (Do you like pozole?). You can also ask about someone else: "¿Le gustan las enchiladas?" (Does he like enchiladas?). There is no word for do in Spanish questions, so do not try to translate it.

Answer with the same pattern. "Sí, me gusta" or "No, no me gusta." Notice the double no. The first one answers the question. The second one makes the verb negative. That double no sounds strange to English ears but is perfectly correct Spanish. Practice both answers aloud with a partner.

words.d: I don't like — no goes before the pronoun: No me gusta la cebolla.
do you like…? — informal question to one person: ¿Te gusta el pozole?
spicy food, heat from chile — No le gusta el picante (He doesn't like spicy food)

look.title: Calling the cousins
look.text:
Lucía: ¿Te gustan los tamales de rajas? (Do you like tamales with chile strips?)
Primo: Sí, me gustan mucho. (Yes, I like them a lot.)
Lucía: ¿Y te gusta el picante?
Primo: No, no me gusta. (No, I don't like it.)
look.prompt: Ask a partner two questions with ¿Te gusta…? and ¿Te gustan…?, and answer theirs.

check.q: How do you say "I don't like onions"?
check.why: No goes before me, and las cebollas is plural, so the verb is gustan.

check.q: How do you ask a friend "Do you like to dance?"
check.why: Te means to you (informal), and an infinitive takes gusta.

check.q: Why does the answer "No, no me gusta" have two no's?
choices: It is a mistake; one no is enough.
The first answers the question; the second makes the verb negative.
Two no's make a positive, like in math.
The second no means not very much.
check.why: The first no is the answer; the second no, before me gusta, makes the sentence negative.

lessons.title: The Six Pronouns
lessons.mainIdea: The person who likes something is shown by me, te, le, nos, os or les before the verb.
reading: Lucía's notebook needs a line for everyone. For herself: *me* gusta. For her cousin: te gusta. For Abuela: le gusta. For herself and Tomás: nos gusta. For the twins: les gusta. These are the *indirect object pronouns*, and they tell who finds the thing pleasing.

Here is the full set: me (to me), te (to you, informal), *le* (to him, to her, to you formal), nos (to us), os (to you all, informal in Spain), *les* (to them, to you all). Notice that le and les cover several people each. Le can mean him, her or usted.

The verb stays gusta or gustan no matter which pronoun you use. "Les gusta el arroz" (They like rice) and "Me gusta el arroz" (I like rice) share the same verb, because the rice is the subject in both. Only the pronoun changes. Only the small pronoun in front changes.

words.d: to me, to you (informal) — Me gusta. ¿Te gusta?
to him, to her, to you (usted) — Le gusta el mole.
to us; to you all (informal, mostly Spain) — Nos gusta. Os gusta.
to them, to you all (ustedes) — Les gustan los tamales.

look.title: Lucía's family chart
look.text:
Lucía → me gusta el pozole
Tomás (to him directly) → te gusta el pozole
Abuela → le gusta el mole
Lucía y Tomás → nos gustan los tamales
las gemelas → les gusta el pastel
look.prompt: Make the same chart for four people in your own family and one food each.

check.q: Which pronoun completes the sentence? A mis padres ___ gusta el café.
check.why: Mis padres is plural (them), so the pronoun is les.

check.q: What does "Nos gustan las películas de terror" mean?
check.why: Nos means to us, so the sentence means we like horror movies.

check.q: Which sentence means "She likes the song"?
check.why: To her is le, and la canción is singular, so the verb is gusta.

lessons.title: A Mí, A Ti, A Ella
lessons.mainIdea: A phrase like a mí, a ti or a Abuela adds emphasis or makes clear who le or les refers to.
reading: "Le gusta el mole" could mean he, she or you (usted) likes mole. To make it clear, add a plus the person at the start: "A Abuela le gusta el mole." You can use a name, a noun or a pronoun: a ella, a él, a usted, a mis tíos. This a phrase usually comes first in the sentence.

The pronouns after a are *a mí* (with an accent), a ti (no accent), a él, a ella, a usted, a nosotros, a vosotros, a ellos, a ellas, a ustedes. They add emphasis or contrast: "A mí me gusta el pozole, pero a ti te gusta el menudo" (I like pozole, but you like menudo).

Here is the catch: the a phrase is added, not swapped. You still need the small pronoun. "A mí gusta" is wrong; it must be "A mí me gusta." Also, mí needs its accent. Without it, mi means my, as in mi casa. That accent is the whole difference. Check both every time you write a mí.

words.d: to me, for emphasis — A mí me gusta. Mí has an accent; mi (my) does not.
to you (informal), for emphasis — A ti te gusta. No accent on ti.
to him / to her — clears up who le means: A ella le gusta.

look.title: Clearing up le
look.text:
Le gusta el mole. (Who? Him? Her? You?)
A Abuela le gusta el mole. (Grandma likes mole.)
A tío Raúl no le gusta el picante. (Uncle Raúl doesn't like spicy food.)
A usted le gusta el café, ¿verdad? (You like coffee, right?)
look.prompt: Write two sentences that contrast what you like with what a friend likes, using a mí and a ti.

check.q: Which sentence is correct?
choices: A mi me gusta la pizza.
A mí me gusta la pizza.
check.why: The a phrase adds emphasis but does not replace me, and mí needs its accent.

check.q: Which phrase makes clear that le means your teacher?
choices: A la profesora le gusta leer.
A la profesora les gusta leer.
check.why: Use a plus the person, and keep the pronoun le for one person.

check.q: Which pronoun completes the sentence? A mis primos ___ gustan los videojuegos.
check.why: Mis primos means them, so the pronoun is les.

lessons.title: Me Too, Me Neither
lessons.mainIdea: Agree with a positive using a mí también, and with a negative using a mí tampoco.
reading: Tomás says, "Me gusta el pastel de tres leches." Lucía agrees: "*A mí también*" (Me too). Because gustar is not a yo verb, you cannot say "yo también" here in careful Spanish. The answer matches the a mí form of the sentence. "Yo también" is heard in casual speech, but a mí también matches the grammar.

When the first sentence is negative, the agreement changes. "No me gusta la cebolla." "*A mí tampoco*" (Me neither). Tampoco means neither or not either. Answering a negative with también is a common mistake. It would mean you DO like it, which is the opposite of agreeing.

To disagree, flip it. If someone says "Me gusta el menudo" and you don't, answer "A mí no." If someone says "No me gusta el menudo" and you do, answer "A mí sí." Four little answers cover every case: también, tampoco, no and sí. Practice them with a partner until they feel automatic.

words.d: me too — agrees with a positive gustar sentence
me neither — agrees with a negative gustar sentence

words.w: a mí sí / a mí no
words.d: I do / I don't — disagrees with what someone else said

look.title: Four answers
look.text:
Me gusta el menudo. → Agree: A mí también. Disagree: A mí no.
No me gusta el menudo. → Agree: A mí tampoco. Disagree: A mí sí.
look.prompt: Your friend says "No me gustan las matemáticas." Answer twice: once agreeing, once disagreeing.

check.q: Your friend says "No me gusta el frío." You agree. What do you say?
check.why: To agree with a negative, use tampoco: a mí tampoco.

check.q: Your friend says "Me gustan los perros." You don't like dogs. What do you say?
check.why: To disagree with a positive, say a mí no.

check.q: What does "A mí también" mean?
check.why: También means also or too, so a mí también means me too.

lessons.title: Encantar: To Love Something
lessons.mainIdea: Encantar works exactly like gustar and means to love a thing or activity: me encanta el mole.
reading: Abuela does more than like mole. "Le encanta el mole" (She loves mole). *Encantar* (to delight, to love a thing) follows the same pattern as gustar. The thing loved is the subject: encanta for one thing or an activity, encantan for many. "Me encantan los tamales" means I love tamales.

Because encantar already means very much, do not add mucho. "Me encanta mucho" is a learner habit carried over from me gusta mucho. Native speakers usually just say me encanta. Also, for people you love, use querer: "Quiero a mi abuela" (I love my grandmother).

Here is a scale from low to high. "No me gusta" (I don't like it), "Me gusta" (I like it), "Me gusta mucho" (I like it a lot), "Me encanta" (I love it). Choosing the right step makes your Spanish sound more natural and more precise. Try placing your own favorite foods on this scale.

words.d: to delight, to love (a thing or activity) — Me encanta bailar. Me encantan los tamales.
to like a lot — Me gusta mucho el arroz.
to love a person — Quiero a mi familia.

look.title: How much?
look.text:
No me gusta la cebolla. (I don't like onion.)
Me gusta el arroz. (I like rice.)
Me gustan mucho los frijoles. (I like beans a lot.)
Me encanta el pastel de tres leches. (I love tres leches cake.)
look.prompt: Rank four foods on the scale from no me gusta to me encanta.

check.q: Which form completes the sentence? A mi hermano le ___ los videojuegos.
check.why: Los videojuegos is plural, so encantar takes encantan.

check.q: How do you say "I love my grandmother"?
check.why: For people you love, Spanish uses querer a, not encantar.

check.q: Which sentence shows the strongest liking?
check.why: Encantar is stronger than gustar; it means to love an activity.

lessons.title: Interesar and Molestar
lessons.mainIdea: Interesar (to interest) and molestar (to bother) follow the gustar pattern: me interesa la historia; me molesta el ruido.
reading: The twins do not like onion. More precisely, "Les molesta la cebolla" (The onion bothers them). *Molestar* (to bother) puts the annoying thing first as the subject. Loud music, homework, a long line: whatever bothers you is the subject of molestar. "Me molesta el tráfico" means traffic bothers me.

*Interesar* (to interest) works the same way. "Me interesa la historia de México" (Mexican history interests me). "¿Te interesan los deportes?" (Are you interested in sports?). English also uses this order: History interests me. That can make interesar feel easier than gustar.

Watch the plural. "Me molestan los mosquitos" (Mosquitoes bother me) takes the n because los mosquitos is plural. And watch the meaning of molestar. It means to bother or annoy, not the English word molest. False friends like this can cause real embarrassment.

words.d: to interest — Me interesa el arte. ¿Te interesan las ciencias?
to bother, annoy — Me molesta el ruido. A false friend: not the English molest.
the noise, the sound

look.title: What bothers, what interests
look.text:
A Tomás le molesta el tráfico. (Traffic bothers Tomás.)
A Lucía le interesan las recetas. (Recipes interest Lucía.)
A las gemelas les molesta la cebolla. (Onion bothers the twins.)
Nos interesa la música mexicana. (Mexican music interests us.)
look.prompt: Name one thing that bothers you and one that interests you, using me molesta and me interesa.

check.q: Which form completes the sentence? Me ___ los ruidos fuertes.
check.why: Los ruidos fuertes is plural, so molestar takes molestan.

check.q: What does "No me interesa el béisbol" mean?
check.why: Interesar means to interest; me means to me, so the sentence means I'm not interested in baseball.

check.q: What does molestar mean?
check.why: Molestar means to bother or annoy. It is a false friend of the English word molest.

lessons.title: Faltar: What's Missing
lessons.mainIdea: Faltar means to be missing or lacking, and the missing thing is the subject: nos falta el postre.
reading: At the end of the story, Tomás says, "Nos falta el postre" (We're missing dessert). *Faltar* (to be missing, to lack) follows the gustar pattern. Word by word, it says Dessert is missing to us. The missing thing is the subject. It is the same pattern with a new meaning.

One thing: falta. More than one: faltan. "Me faltan dos platos" (I'm missing two plates, I need two more plates). "¿Qué te falta?" (What do you need? What are you missing?). You will hear this at stores, in kitchens and when a teacher counts papers. Faltar is everywhere.

Faltar also shows how much remains. "Faltan diez minutos" (There are ten minutes left) uses no pronoun at all. Minutes are the subject. English speakers often reach for necesitar, which is fine, but faltar is what native speakers use for something missing from a set.

words.d: to be missing, to lack — Nos falta el postre. Me faltan dos platos.
the dessert
to need — a regular -ar verb: necesito, necesitas, necesita

look.title: Setting the table for twenty
look.text:
Tomás: Tenemos dieciocho sillas. (We have eighteen chairs.)
Lucía: Somos veinte. Nos faltan dos sillas. (There are twenty of us. We're missing two chairs.)
Tomás: ¿Y los platos?
Lucía: Nos falta uno. (We're missing one.)
look.prompt: You are packing for a trip. Say two things you are missing with me falta and me faltan.

check.q: Which form completes the sentence? Nos ___ tres sillas.
check.why: Tres sillas is plural and is the subject, so faltar takes faltan.

check.q: What does "Me falta el lápiz" mean?
check.why: Faltar means to be missing: the pencil is missing to me.

check.q: Which sentence is correct?
check.why: Cinco minutos is plural and is the subject, so the verb is faltan.

lessons.title: Talking About Hobbies
lessons.mainIdea: Combine gustar, encantar and interesar with infinitives to describe hobbies and ask about someone else's.
reading: At the party, cousins who haven't met in a year catch up. "¿Qué te gusta hacer?" (What do you like to do?). This question is the heart of every getting-to-know-you conversation. Hacer means to do, and it stays an infinitive after gusta. "¿Qué le gusta hacer?" is the polite version.

Answers use the verbs from this chapter with infinitives: "Me encanta dibujar" (I love to draw). "Me interesa aprender a cocinar" (I'm interested in learning to cook). You can also add nouns: "Me gusta la música de banda" (I like banda music). Remember: infinitives take the singular verb.

Keep the conversation going by asking back. "¿Y a ti?" (And you?) turns any statement into a question. For an adult, use usted: "¿Y a usted, tía, qué le gusta hacer?" (And you, Aunt, what do you like to do?). The le shows respect, just as usted does.

words.d: what do you like to do? — the classic question about hobbies
and you? — informal; with an adult, ¿y a usted?
the hobby, pastime — Mi pasatiempo favorito es leer.

look.title: Cousins catching up
look.text:
Lucía: ¿Qué te gusta hacer, Sofía?
Sofía: Me encanta nadar. ¿Y a ti?
Lucía: A mí me gusta cocinar. Me interesan las recetas de Abuela.
Sofía: ¡A mí también!
look.prompt: Write a four-line dialogue with a classmate about hobbies. Use ¿y a ti? at least once.

check.q: How do you ask your aunt what she likes to do, politely?
check.why: For usted, the pronoun is le: ¿Qué le gusta hacer?

check.q: Which sentence is correct?
check.why: Infinitives count as one thing, so the verb is encanta.

check.q: Your friend says "Me gusta nadar." How do you ask the same question back?
check.why: ¿Y a ti? (And you?) turns the statement back to your friend.

review.q: Which form completes the sentence? A Lucía le ___ las enchiladas.
review.why: Las enchiladas is plural and is the subject, so the verb is gustan.
The thing liked is the subject (la música, singular), and the person is me.

review.q: Which pronoun completes the sentence? A nosotros ___ encanta la playa.
review.why: A nosotros means to us, so the pronoun is nos.

review.q: Your friend says "No me gustan los lunes." You agree. What do you say?
review.why: To agree with a negative, use a mí tampoco.

review.q: What does "Les molesta el ruido" mean?
review.why: Molestar means to bother, and les means to them.

review.q: Which form completes the sentence? Me ___ dos libros para la clase.
review.why: Dos libros is plural and is the subject, so faltar takes faltan.

review.q: Why is "A mi me gusta" missing something?
choices: It needs yo at the start.
It needs gustan instead of gusta.
Mí needs an accent to mean me instead of my.
review.why: After a, the pronoun is mí with an accent; mi without the accent means my.

review.q: In the story, why does Lucía say gusta for el arroz but gustan for los tamales?
choices: Because the verb agrees with the thing liked, one or many
review.why: Gustar agrees with its subject, the thing liked: one thing takes gusta, many take gustan.
